meta.name: 110 - En Route Delivery with Shoulder Dystocia

patient.name: Marisol Vega
patient.chiefComplaint: Lower back pain, thought to be muscular strain

history.hpi: G4P3 patient at 38 weeks gestation reports lower back pain for the past hour that she attributes to helping move boxes earlier in the day. Denies 'contractions' in her own words, but on direct questioning describes cyclical tightening across her lower abdomen roughly every 6-8 minutes. Each of her three prior pregnancies progressed from first noticeable contraction to delivery in under 90 minutes. Denies rupture of membranes or bloody show at this time. Denies urge to push.
pastMedical: Three prior spontaneous vaginal deliveries, all uncomplicated and rapid
Gestational hypertension during second pregnancy, resolved postpartum
history.events: Patient called EMS for worsening back pain; declined to have her husband drive her given how quickly her prior labors progressed

scene.location: Two-story home, main-floor living room; patient slowly pacing, one hand braced on the small of her back
scene.bystanders: Husband present; will follow behind in the family vehicle
visualCues: Patient pacing slowly, periodically pausing and breathing through discomfort
No visible perineal bulging or crowning on initial exam
A packed overnight bag labeled 'hospital bag' sits by the front door
Patient declines to lie supine on the stretcher, prefers side-lying

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 35-year-old G4P3 female at 38 weeks gestation, ambulatory and uncomfortable with lower back pain she attributes to lifting earlier in the day. She denies contractions by name but describes a cyclical tightening pattern when questioned directly.

otherFindings: Lower back pain 5/10, cyclical, waxing and waning
No vaginal bleeding or fluid noted
Fundal height consistent with late third trimester
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It's probably just my back from moving boxes earlier — I don't think this is labor, but with my other three it went fast."

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain focused OB history: gravida/para, gestational age, contraction pattern, membrane/bleeding status
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: OB assessment: Length of pregnancy Number of pregnancies Number of viable births Number of non-viable births Due date (calculate gestational age in weeks) Signs of imminent delivery (e.g., crowning, urge to push, urge to move bowels, mother feels delivery is imminent)
expectedActions.rationale: A rapid multiparous history with no imminent-delivery signs guides the on-scene-versus-transport decision.

expectedActions.shortAction: No crowning or urge to push present; begin transport to the receiving facility
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If patient in labor but no signs of imminent delivery, transport to appropriate receiving facility
expectedActions.rationale: Given her history of rapid prior labors, prompt transport reduces the risk of delivering without hospital resources available.

transitions.condition: Crew obtains a focused OB history (gravida/para, gestational age, contraction pattern, membrane/bleeding status) and finds no signs of imminent delivery, beginning non-emergent transport per protocol.

phases.name: OB history obtained, transport initiated
phases.description: Crew completes a focused OB assessment. Contractions are present but irregular in the patient's perception; there is no crowning, urge to push, or bloody show. Per protocol, the crew begins transport toward the receiving facility rather than delaying on scene.
phases.triggerCondition: After the focused OB history confirms active labor without signs of imminent delivery, the crew loads the patient and begins transport, continuing periodic reassessment en route.

otherFindings: Contractions now timed at roughly 5 minutes apart, 40-50 seconds duration
No crowning on brief visual exam
Patient positioned left-lateral on the stretcher for comfort
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Okay, these are closer together than I thought. Let's just get going."

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize crowning and urge to push; commit to delivering in the moving ambulance
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Signs of imminent delivery: Crowning or other presentation in vaginal opening Urge to push Urge to move bowels Mother's sense of imminent delivery
expectedActions.rationale: Delivery cannot be delayed once crowning and pushing urge are present; committing early avoids an unassisted, unprepared birth.

transitions.condition: Partway through transport, the patient suddenly reports an overwhelming urge to push; reassessment reveals crowning, indicating imminent delivery inside the moving ambulance.

phases.name: Crowning discovered en route
phases.description: Mid-transport, the patient reports a sudden, overwhelming urge to push. Reassessment in the moving compartment reveals crowning — delivery is now imminent and will not wait for hospital arrival.
phases.triggerCondition: The patient's contractions intensify rapidly during transport; on reassessment she is crowning, consistent with her history of very short labors, forcing the crew to prepare for delivery inside the moving ambulance rather than continuing to the hospital.

otherFindings: Crowning visible with contractions
Strong involuntary urge to push
Contractions now less than 2 minutes apart
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It's coming right now, I can't stop it — the baby's coming!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Open the delivery kit and support the infant's head with gentle counterpressure as it emerges
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Delivery should be controlled to allow a slow controlled delivery of infant – This will prevent injury to mother. Support the infant's head as needed and apply gentle counterpressure to help prevent the head from suddenly popping out
expectedActions.rationale: Preparing the kit and controlling head delivery in a moving compartment prevents rapid, uncontrolled expulsion.

transitions.condition: The crew prepares the delivery kit and supports the head with counterpressure as it delivers, maintaining a controlled technique despite the moving compartment.
The crew continues driving at normal speed and does not open the delivery kit or brace for delivery; the infant begins to deliver suddenly and unassisted.

phases.name: Delivery prepared, controlled technique used
phases.description: The head delivers under controlled technique, but the anterior shoulder fails to descend with gentle downward guidance — shoulder dystocia is recognized and managed in the confined ambulance compartment.
phases.triggerCondition: The head delivers with controlled counterpressure, but after restitution the anterior shoulder does not deliver with gentle traction. Shoulder dystocia is recognized, requiring immediate maneuvers.

otherFindings: Fetal head delivered and restituted, but anterior shoulder does not descend with gentle traction ('turtle sign')
No nuchal cord identified
Crew repositioning mother in the confined ambulance compartment

expectedActions.shortAction: Check for nuchal cord after head delivers; slip over head if present
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check for nuchal cord (i.e., around the baby's neck) If present, slip it over the head If unable to free the cord from the neck, double clamp the cord and cut between the clamps
expectedActions.rationale: Nuchal cord must be ruled out or managed before proceeding with shoulder delivery.

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize shoulder dystocia; perform McRoberts maneuver, hyperflexing maternal hips
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If delivery fails to progress after head delivers, quickly attempt the following: Hyperflex mother's hips to severe supine knee-chest position (i.e., McRoberts' maneuver)
expectedActions.rationale: McRoberts positioning is the first-line maneuver to resolve shoulder dystocia and should be attempted immediately.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply firm suprapubic pressure with a second crew member to dislodge the shoulder
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Apply firm suprapubic pressure to attempt to dislodge shoulder. This often requires two EMS clinicians to perform and allows for delivery in up to 75% of cases
expectedActions.rationale: Suprapubic pressure combined with McRoberts resolves the majority of shoulder dystocia cases in the field.

transitions.condition: McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure successfully dislodge the anterior shoulder, and delivery completes without further complication.
Instead of performing McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the crew applies direct axial traction on the fetal head in an attempt to free the shoulder.

phases.name: Shoulder delivered, newborn emerges
phases.description: The shoulder dystocia resolves with McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure; the newborn delivers, is dried and warmed, and the crew continues transport while completing postpartum care for both patients.
phases.triggerCondition: After the anterior shoulder is delivered, the remainder of the newborn delivers without further complication. The newborn is dried, warmed, and stimulated while the crew continues toward the hospital.

otherFindings: Newborn delivered, vigorous cry, pink centrally with acrocyanosis
APGAR 8 at 1 minute, improving
Placenta not yet delivered; fundus being monitored
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Oh thank god, is she okay? Is she crying, that's good right?"

expectedActions.shortAction: Clamp cord after 1 minute, cutting between two clamps 5-6 inches from the abdomen
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: After 1 minute, clamp cord about 5–6 inches from the abdomen with two clamps; cut the cord between the clamps
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed cord clamping for one minute benefits the newborn before cutting.

expectedActions.shortAction: Dry, warm, and stimulate newborn; record APGAR scores at 1 and 5 minutes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Dry, warm, and stimulate infant, wrap in towel and place on maternal chest unless resuscitation needed. Record APGAR scores at 1 and 5 minutes once neonate is stabilized
expectedActions.rationale: Warming and stimulation prevent neonatal hypothermia while APGAR scoring tracks transition to extrauterine life.

expectedActions.shortAction: Massage uterine fundus after placenta delivers to promote contraction and control bleeding
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: After delivery, massaging the uterus (should be located at about the umbilicus) and allowing the infant to nurse will promote uterine contraction and help control bleeding
expectedActions.rationale: Fundal massage reduces postpartum hemorrhage risk after a dystocia-complicated delivery.

phases.name: Delivery attempted without preparation
phases.description: The crew continues driving at normal speed without opening the delivery kit or bracing for an in-compartment birth. The infant begins to deliver suddenly and unassisted, creating a risk of dropping the newborn in the moving vehicle.
phases.triggerCondition: Because the crew did not prepare for delivery after crowning was identified, the infant begins delivering rapidly and unassisted while the ambulance is still moving, with no towel or hands positioned to receive the newborn.

otherFindings: Infant delivering rapidly with no towel or supportive hands positioned
Crew scrambling to reach gloves and delivery kit mid-delivery
High risk of dropping the slippery newborn in the moving compartment
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "It's coming, it's coming right now — catch her!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize the drop risk; immediately secure the newborn with both hands and a towel
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Newborns are very slippery, take care not to drop the infant
expectedActions.rationale: An unprepared, unbraced delivery in a moving vehicle sharply increases the risk of dropping a slippery newborn.

phases.name: Head pulled instead of McRoberts
phases.description: Rather than performing McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure, the crew applies direct traction on the fetal head in an attempt to free the shoulder, risking brachial plexus injury to the newborn.
phases.triggerCondition: When the anterior shoulder fails to deliver, the crew pulls axially on the fetal head instead of repositioning the mother and applying suprapubic pressure, directly contradicting the protocol's explicit warning against traction.

otherFindings: Traction applied directly to fetal head with the shoulder still impacted
No improvement in shoulder descent with traction alone
Risk of brachial plexus/clavicular injury to the newborn rising with continued pulling

expectedActions.shortAction: Stop traction on the head immediately; reposition to McRoberts and apply suprapubic pressure
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Attempt to angle baby's head as posteriorly as possible but NEVER pull
expectedActions.rationale: Traction on the head during shoulder dystocia risks brachial plexus injury and must stop immediately in favor of McRoberts and suprapubic pressure.
